items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The variety of English treated as the norm in education, publishing and formal contexts"?
items.answer: Standard English
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of Standard English.

items.stem: Explain the difference between dialect and accent.
items.answer: Accent refers only to pronunciation; dialect includes vocabulary and grammar as well as pronunciation.
items.markingKey: Accent refers only to pronunciation; dialect includes vocabulary and grammar as well as pronunciation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a city mayor at the opening of a public library in a multilingual neighbourhood.

Friends, neighbours – bienvenidos, karibu, welcome. Some people say libraries are relics, that everything we need is on our phones. But a phone cannot hold a child's hand through her first chapter book. A phone does not stay open late for the night-shift nurse who wants to finish her degree. This building belongs to you: to every language spoken on these streets, and to every language not yet learned.

How does the writer's use of language reflect identity in this text?
items.answer: Greeting the audience in several languages before English treats each community's language as equally welcome; it signals that language is part of identity and civic belonging.
items.markingKey: Greeting the audience in several languages before English treats each community's language as equally welcome; it signals that language is part of identity and civic belonging. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Isabel writes: "Dialects are incorrect versions of English." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Dialects are rule-governed systems; "standard" status is social, not linguistic superiority.
items.markingKey: Dialects are rule-governed systems; "standard" status is social, not linguistic superiority. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following post from a travel blog written by a young backpacker in Vietnam.

Day 12. Hanoi. Honestly? I came for the Instagram shots – the lanterns, the train street, the egg coffee. What I got was Mrs Lan, who runs a tiny noodle stall and refused to let me pay because I tried (badly) to say 'thank you' in Vietnamese. Lesson learned: the best stuff here isn't on any list. #slowtravel

Evaluate how the text challenges or reinforces attitudes to non-standard language.
items.answer: The informal register, minor sentences ("Day 12. Hanoi."), colloquial diction and hashtag reflect digital conventions; the attempted Vietnamese "thank you" shows language as a gesture of respect.
items.markingKey: The informal register, minor sentences ("Day 12. Hanoi."), colloquial diction and hashtag reflect digital conventions; the attempted Vietnamese "thank you" shows language as a gesture of respect. Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Schools should teach only Standard English."
items.answer: Standard English should be taught as a tool alongside respect for students' home varieties.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it is needed for formal contexts and exams; it enables wider communication. Arguments against: it can stigmatise students' home varieties; multilingual and multidialectal skills are valuable. Supported judgement: Standard English should be taught as a tool alongside respect for students' home varieties.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "dialect".
items.answer: A variety of a language with distinctive vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation, associated with a region or social group

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "code-switching"?
options: Moving between two or more languages or varieties within a conversation or text
The value speakers place on non-standard varieties as markers of group belonging
A variety of a language with distinctive vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation, associated with a region or social group
A language or variety associated with authority, such as a colonial language or a dominant national language
items.answer: Moving between two or more languages or varieties within a conversation or text
items.markingKey: A. "code-switching" is moving between two or more languages or varieties within a conversation or text.

items.stem: Distinguish between borrowing and code-switching.
items.answer: Code-switching alternates between languages in discourse; borrowing adopts single words from one language into another as part of its vocabulary (e.g. "café").

items.stem:
Read the following letter to the editor of a regional newspaper in northern England.

Sir, – Your columnist last week described our local accent as 'charming but unprofessional'. I have been a nurse for twenty-two years. I have said 'you're alright, love' to frightened patients at three in the morning, and not one has asked for my vowels to be adjusted. Accent is not a skill deficit. It is where we come from, and where many of your readers still live.

How does language mixing in this text relate to identity or power?
items.answer: The dialect endearment "you're alright, love" is presented as professional comfort; the writer argues that accent marks regional and class identity and that judging it is prejudice.

items.stem:
Read the following meme shared on a student forum, described in words.

[Image, top: a tiny kitten stares bravely at an enormous, overflowing laundry basket. Top text: 'ME IN SEPTEMBER: I'LL START MY IA EARLY THIS YEAR'.]
[Image, bottom: the same kitten, now buried under the laundry, only its ears showing. Bottom text: 'ME, 11:58 P.M. THE NIGHT BEFORE THE DEADLINE'.]

Analyse how dialect, accent or a variety of English is presented in this text.
items.answer: The template "ME IN ... / ALSO ME" is a recognisable meme formula; in-group acronyms and capitals mark the language of online student communities.

items.stem:
Read the following advertisement for a family SUV, printed in a weekend newspaper magazine.

[Image: a father at the wheel, two children asleep in the back, mountains at dusk through the windscreen.]
HE'S GOT THIS.
Seven seats. Five-star safety. Zero doubts.
The Atlas X7. Built for the man who carries everyone.
[Small print: 7.9 L/100 km combined. Model shown with optional extras.]

How does the text represent gender?
items.answer: The man is represented as protector and driver and the children as passive passengers; the mother is absent, and the pronoun "He" in the headline assumes the driver and carer is male, reinforcing a traditional provider role.
items.markingKey: The man is represented as protector and driver and the children as passive passengers; the mother is absent, and the pronoun "He" in the headline assumes the driver and carer is male, reinforcing a traditional provider role. items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Schools should teach only Standard English."
items.answer: Standard English should be taught as a tool alongside respect for students' home varieties.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it is needed for formal contexts and exams; it enables wider communication. Arguments against: it can stigmatise students' home varieties; multilingual and multidialectal skills are valuable. Supported judgement: Standard English should be taught as a tool alongside respect for students' home varieties. Markbands (10 marks): Markbands (criteria A–D). items.stem: "Advertising today challenges gender stereotypes more than it reinforces them." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Advertising has shifted but often repackages stereotypes; the change is partial and commercially motivated.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: many brands promote diversity; regulators have banned harmful stereotypes in some countries. Arguments against: many adverts still use traditional roles; "femvertising" can commodify empowerment.
